blocks.content: Avoiding exam traps is as crucial as mastering the syllabus, as negative marking can turn potential ranks into disqualifications.

rows: Hides 'NOT' or 'EXCEPT' within lengthy question stems
Underline/circle negative terms in your first reading pass
Uses 'Only', 'Always', or 'Never' to make false options sound authoritative
Apply extreme skepticism to rigid, unyielding generalizations
Positions a partially correct answer at Option A to exploit rush
Mandatorily read all options (A to D) before filling OMR/clicking
Gives input in one metric system and requests answer in another
Write down given and required units explicitly before calculating

items: Always circle or underline words like 'NOT', 'INCORRECT', and 'FALSE' before analyzing options.
Never select 'All of the above' without confirming that at least two statements are 100% correct.
Check unit dimensions (e.g., m/s vs km/h, months vs years) in numerical problems before finalizing your answer.
Enforce a strict 60-second skip rule to prevent time-sink questions from sabotaging easier sections.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Question setters frequently embed negative words like 'NOT', 'EXCEPT', and 'INCORRECT' to trigger impulse errors.
Extreme qualifiers such as 'Always', 'Never', and 'Only' usually indicate incorrect statements in general studies papers.
Plausible partial truths are deliberately placed as Option A to trick hasty candidates into marking before reading all choices.
Unit mismatches and dimensional conversion tricks are primary traps used in Quantitative Aptitude and Physics sections.
Adopting a systematic elimination technique significantly reduces exposure to examiner traps under time pressure.
